title: World Cup 2026 Could Cost US Employers $30 Billion in Lost Productivity as Workers Stream Matches From Their Desks
excerpt: With 78 matches across 11 American cities over 39 days, the first US-hosted World Cup in 32 years is disrupting workplace attendance, cancelling meetings, and testing HR policies nationwide.
body:

  • Office attendance dropped 26 percent after the US team's elimination, with visitor entries falling 32 percent and meetings widely cancelled
  • 40 percent of organizations expect workplace disruptions, but 42 percent have no plans in place to manage them
  • HR experts recommend embracing the tournament through watch parties and flexible scheduling rather than fighting it

The $30 Billion Match Day

The 2026 FIFA World Cup has been a bonanza for fans and host cities, drawing more than five million in-person attendees and an estimated six billion viewers worldwide. For American employers, the numbers tell a different story.

An analysis from outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas found that if every employed American who follows soccer took a single day off to watch a marquee match, the cost to US employers would reach $30.2 billion in lost productivity. Even a single hour of distraction across the workforce carries a price tag of roughly $4.4 billion.

With 78 matches scheduled across 11 American cities over 39 days — the first time the US has hosted a World Cup since 1994 — the disruption has been sustained and unavoidable. Unlike a single-afternoon tournament bracket, the World Cup's group stages, knockout rounds, and semifinals have landed squarely on weekday afternoons, giving workers repeated opportunities to step away from their desks.

Meetings Cancelled, Not Just Workers Missing

A workplace analytics report from Envoy found that the biggest disruption came not from workers staying home but from cancelled and postponed meetings. After the US team's elimination, overall office attendance dropped 26 percent, but the decline in visitor entries was even steeper — down 32 percent nationally. Scheduled visitor traffic fell between 26 and 38 percent across every region tracked.

States including Georgia, Michigan, New Jersey, and Tennessee recorded some of the largest declines relative to their normal attendance levels. The data suggests employees largely continued reporting to work, while organizations pulled back on client meetings, interviews, and vendor visits on match days.

"A lost hour of productivity isn't really lost if you get it back in goodwill, retention, and a team that actually wants to come in on Monday."

— Andy Challenger, Chief Revenue Officer, Challenger, Gray & Christmas

Host Cities Buck the Trend

World Cup host cities told a different story. According to Envoy, Seattle operated close to normal on the day it hosted the US match before recording its weakest weekday attendance the following morning, down 20.4 percent. Los Angeles and Dallas both exceeded or matched their normal attendance baselines while hosting matches. The data suggests matches actually increased activity within host cities as local economies benefited from the influx of fans.

Lean In, Don't Fight It

Brightmine, an HR analytics platform, found that 40 percent of organizations expected workplace disruptions during the tournament — but 42 percent had no plans in place to manage them. Several HR firms have released workplace guides advising employers to channel the tournament's energy rather than suppress it.

"Smart employers won't try to fight it. They'll build it into the schedule," said Andy Challenger. "The companies that turn this into a team-building moment — watch parties, flexible hours, brackets — will protect morale and probably get more real productivity out of the day."

For Indian-American professionals, who represent one of the largest groups in US tech and corporate workplaces, the World Cup has offered a rare moment of shared cultural excitement. With India's growing engagement in global football fandom and the diaspora's deep roots in American corporate life, the tournament has become a breakroom conversation starter that cuts across teams and time zones. As the final weekend approaches — France vs. England on Saturday, Argentina vs. Spain on Sunday — the last burst of disruption may also be the most productive: the shared experience of watching together.
